newsitem.title: USA: Budget negotiators agree to give talks more time.
newsitem.headline: Budget negotiators agree to give talks more time.

text.p: The White House and Congress agreed Thursday to give budget negotiations more time, even though there was no deal cut in this "make it or break it" week.
"There was no saber rattling yesterday or today," Democratic Rep. John Spratt of South Carolina said when asked what progress had been made in the nearly two weeks of talks.
"We may shock you in the next five or six days," Senate Budget Committee chairman Pete Domenici, a New Mexico Republican, told reporters after the day's session concluded.

President Clinton sent Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin to argue for his funding requests for international affairs and U.S. contributions to international development.
But outside the closed-door talks, some Democrats warned their party's budget negotiators against accepting spending cuts in domestic programs.
Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle, Democrat of South Dakota, said Republicans needed to make more concessions before Democrats offer up more spending cuts.
Domenici, who had given the "make it or break it" name to this week, said he had no plans to broker a separate budget agreement between Republicans and conservative Democrats.
"I prefer to see if we can get the president on board and I think he wants to be on board... We want to give it a few more days," Domenici said.

The two sides are trying to reach agreement on spending cuts that would bring the federal deficit to zero by 2002 and to provide some tax relief during the five years. The deficit stood at $107 billion in the last fiscal year, but burgeoning costs of retirement and health programs threaten to push it to record levels unless programs are changed.

Clinton's chief negotiator, Office of Management and Budget Director Frank Raines, said he did not underestimate the difficulty of reaching a final deal. "I think everybody acknowledges we are making progress and we hope we can bring it to conclusion," he said. But Raines cautioned, "There is absolutely no guarantee that we can bring it to a successful conclusion."

The budget talks will resume Wednesday. At that time, negotiators may reconsider some of the thornier budget issues -- ways to slow down the growth in Medicare and Medicaid health programs and the gap between Republican and Democratic tax cut proposals.
Clinton has sought a $98 billion income tax cut, chiefly paid for with increases in other types of taxes and by closing loopholes. Republicans have suggested some $177 billion in tax cuts.
